body.text:
My granddaughter rescued me from my own bathroom on a Saturday afternoon and I haven't told a single person in my family the real reason.

Not my husband. Not my daughter. Not my sister who calls me every Sunday at 4 PM like clockwork.

The reason is that I couldn't turn the doorknob.

Not jammed. Not locked. Not stuck. The knob worked fine. My hand didn't.

Six years old. That's how old Maddie was when she pushed the spare key through the gap under the door and I knelt down on the bath mat in my own house and used the side of my palm to slide it toward me because I couldn't make my fingers close around it.

I want to tell you the rest of this story because I think there are women reading this who are going to recognize themselves in it. Not the bathroom part. The other part. The part where you stop telling people things. The part where you start doing math about what you can still do and what you can't.

My name is Brenda. I'm 57 years old. I live in Chattanooga, Tennessee, on the side of Signal Mountain where the road gets steep and the deer eat my hostas every spring. I taught second grade in Hamilton County for 28 years. I retired in 2022 because my hands stopped letting me write on the whiteboard for longer than 5 minutes at a stretch and I couldn't open the markers anymore without asking a 7 year old to do it for me.

My husband Dale is a retired electrician. He still does small jobs for our church and for the neighbors on our street. He's 61 and he could replace a ceiling fan in his sleep.

We have one daughter, Carrie. She lives in East Ridge with her husband Jason and our granddaughter Madeline, who everyone calls Maddie. Maddie was born in July of 2018, which makes her the kind of fearless half pint who climbs trees in church dresses and will eat anything you put in front of her.

Maddie spends Saturdays with me when Carrie has her real estate showings. Has since she was old enough to walk.

That's important.

Because the day my hands betrayed me, she was the only person in the house.

Let me back up.

This didn't start on a Saturday. It started about 4 years ago, slow, the way things start when you're not paying attention.

I noticed it first in the kitchen.

I couldn't open jars. I'd hand them to Dale without saying anything because we have one of those marriages where you don't have to explain. Pickles. Pasta sauce. Mayonnaise. The lid of the maple syrup I bought at the farmer's market every fall from a man with a beard down to his belt buckle.

Dale never said anything about it either. He just opened them.

Then it was buttons.

I have a navy blouse I've owned since 2014. There's a small pearl button at the very top of the collar. One morning I was getting ready for church and I stood in front of the mirror and worked at that button for almost a full minute before I gave up and wore a scarf.

I told myself it was the button. The button was small. The button was old. The button was the problem.

Then it was the steering wheel.

I drive a 2015 Honda CR-V. The wheel is a normal size. But there's a moment when you're turning into a tight parking spot, the kind where you have to hand-over-hand the wheel quickly, where I started losing my grip in the middle of the turn. My hand would slide off the leather instead of pulling through.

I started parking further away in the Publix lot so I wouldn't have to do tight turns.

I'm 57.

You don't think 57 is old. Not when you're 57.

You think 57 is the age your mother was when she was still planting bulbs and going to the beach in Destin with her girlfriends and complaining about your father's golf shoes. 57 is supposed to be the age you finally take that trip to Italy that you've been talking about since 2011.

It isn't supposed to be the age your fingers stop closing.

I went to my doctor in February of 2024. Her name is Dr. Elizabeth Sheppard. She's a good woman. She's been my primary care for 11 years.

She looked at my hands, asked me to make a fist, asked me to grip her two fingers and squeeze.

I squeezed.

She said "yeah, there's some weakness there."

I said "is that normal?"

She said "for your age, some grip loss is pretty common. Probably some osteoarthritis starting up in the smaller joints. We'll keep an eye on it. Try some glucosamine, see if it helps. Lots of water. Try not to grip things so hard."

I drove home from that appointment and sat in my driveway for 14 minutes before I went inside.

Try not to grip things so hard.

She didn't mean it the way it landed. I know she didn't. She's a good woman. She's tired. She has 8 minutes per patient and a waiting room full of people who all want her to fix something she can't fix.

But the way it landed, sitting in that driveway looking at the dogwood Dale planted the year Carrie graduated, was this.

She thinks I'm done.

She thinks this is just what 57 looks like.

She thinks the rest of my life is going to be small jars I can't open and small buttons I can't button and small girls' hair I can't braid and small hands I can't hold the way I want to hold them.

I went inside and I didn't tell Dale about the appointment. I told him she said everything looked fine.

That was a lie.

I started taking the glucosamine. I bought the kind with chondroitin in it because the bottle said it was stronger. I took it every morning with my coffee for 7 months. I bought a grip strengthener at the Sports Authority that closed down 2 weeks later, like the universe was telling me something. I squeezed it while I watched Wheel of Fortune.

Nothing changed.

I bought a different brand. I bought turmeric. I bought collagen powder I mixed into my coffee and pretended I couldn't taste. I bought CBD cream Carrie's hairdresser swore by. I bought magnetic bracelets from a woman at the Chattanooga Market who told me they helped her husband. I bought a paraffin wax machine for my hands that I used for 3 weeks and then put in the back of the bathroom closet.

By November I had a shelf in the pantry that looked like a CVS aisle and hands that still couldn't open a jar of marinara.

I stopped telling Dale what I was trying.

He'd see the new bottle on the counter and not say anything. Sometimes he'd ask "anything helping?" and I'd say "I don't know yet, too soon to tell."

Always too soon to tell.

Then came the Saturday.

It was September 7th of last year. A clear afternoon, 78 degrees, the kind of day where you have the back door cracked open so the dog can come in and out as he pleases. Our dog is a 13 year old yellow lab named Banjo who mostly sleeps under the kitchen table.

Maddie was in the living room watching a cartoon about a family of horses that lived in a barn shaped like a guitar. She had her little legs stretched out across the ottoman and her socks were the kind with cats on them and one of the cats had a tear in its eye from where I'd accidentally caught it in the dryer.

I went to the bathroom around 2:15.

It's the half bath off the kitchen. The one with the white pedestal sink and the embroidered hand towel that says HOME SWEET HOME that my mother in law made me in 2009 and that I will never replace because she died 3 months after she gave it to me.

I closed the door behind me, the way you do.

When I went to leave I couldn't open it.

I want to be precise about this because the precision is the part that wrecked me.

I could put my hand on the knob. I could feel the cool metal under my palm. I could feel the smooth porcelain of the knob's surface. I knew exactly what I needed to do.

My fingers wouldn't close.

It was like trying to make a fist underwater. Like the signal from my brain was leaving on time and getting lost somewhere between my wrist and the second knuckle.

I tried the other hand. Same thing. Worse, actually, because my right has always been my better hand.

I tried with both hands together, palms pressed against the knob like I was praying. My hands slid right off the metal.

The door was not locked. The mechanism worked. The knob turned freely. I just couldn't make my hands turn it.

I stood in that half bath for what felt like a long time but was probably 30 seconds.

Then I heard Maddie call out from the living room.

"GiGi, the show ended."

I'm called GiGi because when she was 2 she couldn't say grandma. It stuck.

I called back through the door, as casual as I could make it, "GiGi's stuck in the bathroom, baby. The door's being silly."

She said "are you stuck stuck?"

I said "kind of."

There was a pause.

Then I heard her little feet on the kitchen tile coming toward me.

She tried the knob from her side. It turned but the door didn't open because there's a quirk in the latch that you have to pull at the same time as you turn. We've meant to fix it for years.

She said "the magic door."

I'd called it that to her once. The magic door. Because you have to know the trick.

She said "GiGi, do you want me to get the key?"

There's a spare key on top of the door frame because that lock has been a problem for 9 years and Dale put one up there a long time ago for exactly this reason. But Maddie can't reach the top of the door frame. She's 3 and a half feet tall.

I said "Maddie. Listen to me. Go to the kitchen drawer next to the silverware. The one with the rubber bands and the take out menus. There's an extra key in that drawer. It's silver. It has a little blue dot on it."

I heard her say "okay" and her feet went toward the kitchen.

I leaned my forehead against the door.

I was crying. Not loud. Quiet. The kind of crying you do when you don't want a child to know.

She came back. I could hear her breathing on the other side of the door. She said "I got it."

I said "good girl. Now I need you to push it under the door to me. Slide it on the floor."

She slid the key under. It came across the tile and stopped about 6 inches from my foot.

I knelt down on the bath mat.

I tried to pick the key up with my fingers and my fingers wouldn't close on something that small.

I used the side of my hand and slid the key toward my chest until it hit the toe of my slipper. I pressed it against the slipper and slid both my hand and the key up the side of the door until I could get it into the lock with both palms cupped around it like I was carrying a hummingbird.

The key went in. I turned it with the heel of my palm.

The door opened.

Maddie was standing there in her cat socks. She was holding her favorite stuffed animal, a fox named Phillip, and she had the most serious look on her face I'd ever seen on a 6 year old.

She said "the magic door is broken, GiGi."

I said "I know, baby."

She said "do you want a hug?"

I sat right down on the kitchen floor and I let her crawl into my lap and I held her with the only part of my arms that still worked properly, the crook of my elbows, and I cried into the top of her head while Banjo padded over and put his nose on my knee.

I have not told Dale.

I have not told Carrie.

I have not told Dr. Sheppard.

I have not told my sister.

For exactly one reason.

If I tell anybody, they will start watching me. Carrie will start hovering. Dale will start opening things before I can try. Dr. Sheppard will refer me to a specialist who will tell me what she already told me, which is that this is "just what 57 looks like."

And the version of me that retired from teaching after 28 years is not ready to be the version of me that gets watched.

I have a granddaughter who climbs trees in church dresses.

I have a husband who I can still beat at gin rummy if he lets me.

I have a list of trips I haven't taken yet and a piano in the front room that I learned to play in 1978 and that I have not been able to play for almost 2 years.

I am not done.

That night, after Carrie picked up Maddie at 6, after Dale fell asleep in his recliner watching the Vols lose to Florida, I sat at the kitchen table with my laptop and I opened a new browser window and I typed in the search bar:

why do my fingers stop working

Then I deleted it. I typed:

stiff fingers grip strength loss 50s

I scrolled through 6 pages of WebMD pages and forums full of women who sounded exactly like me. Then I clicked on a forum thread that had a different kind of comment buried 14 posts deep.

It was a woman in Asheville who said something I'd never heard before.

She said this wasn't really about her hands. It was about her cells. She said she'd been told for 8 years that her hands and her knees were just aging, and then she found out that the actual issue was something called mitochondrial function. Her cells weren't making enough energy to maintain the tissue in her joints. Everything she'd been taking was treating the inflammation or the cartilage or the pain, but nothing was supporting the part of her cells that actually does the maintenance work.

That word stopped me.

Maintenance.

That's what I'd been doing my whole life. Maintenance. Lunches packed. Lesson plans written. Birthdays remembered. Anniversaries celebrated. Doctor appointments scheduled. Christmas cards mailed.

What if my body had been doing the same thing all this time? Maintenance. Quiet, daily maintenance, on the parts of me I never thought about. The cartilage in my knuckles. The fluid in my finger joints. The tendons that close my hand around a coffee mug.

And what if the maintenance crew had just stopped showing up?

I read for 4 hours that night. Until 1:36 AM. Dale snored on the couch and Banjo snored on the rug and I sat at the kitchen table with the under cabinet lights on and I learned things nobody ever told me.

Every cell in your body needs energy to do its job. That energy is made by your mitochondria. Mitochondria are the little engines inside every cell. They're not metaphor. They're real. You learned about them in 8th grade biology and forgot.

The cells in your joints are some of the busiest cells in your body. They have to constantly maintain cartilage, regulate inflammation, keep the joint lubricated, signal when something is wrong, repair small damages from daily use. They need a lot of energy to do all that.

When your mitochondria are working well, those cells get the energy they need to keep up with their job.

When your mitochondria start to slow down, which they do with age, with stress, with processed food, with environmental load, with everything modern life dumps on us, those cells start running on fumes. They can't keep up with maintenance. The cartilage starts thinning. The inflammation signaling goes haywire. The lubrication production drops off. The joint starts to feel it.

The pain isn't the start of the problem.

The pain is the bill coming due for years of unpaid maintenance.

Nobody had ever explained any of it to me that way.

Dr. Sheppard didn't.

My pharmacist didn't.

The bottles in my pantry didn't.

The glucosamine was trying to give the joint more building material. Like dropping off lumber at a construction site. But what good is lumber if the construction crew has been laid off?

The CBD was trying to dial down the pain signal. Useful for the noise. Did nothing for the source.

The collagen powder was the same as the glucosamine. More raw material. No workers.

I'd been delivering lumber to a construction site with no power.

For 4 years.

That's the line that broke me open at 1:36 in the morning. Lumber to a construction site with no power.

I kept reading. I read about something called AMPK. It's a pathway in your cells. Think of it like the master switch on the wall in a factory. When AMPK is active, the whole place lights up. The engines fire. The crew gets to work. When AMPK is sluggish, the lights are dim and the crew is half asleep at their stations.

There's a fruit called amla. Indian gooseberry. I'd never heard of it.

In Ayurvedic medicine in India they call it "the nurse." For thousands of years. The nurse. The thing that quietly takes care of everything else.

It's been studied. In real studies. Not perfect ones, because nothing is perfect, but real ones. Researchers have found that amla helps activate AMPK. It helps turn that master switch back on.

When AMPK is on, your mitochondria can start making energy more efficiently. The way they did when you were 32 and the marinara jar opened on the first twist.

The cells in your joints can finally get the energy they need to do their maintenance work.

The crew comes back.

The amla also has one of the highest antioxidant profiles ever measured in a food. So while it's helping turn the lights back on at the factory, it's also protecting the workers from the wear and tear that was breaking them down in the first place.

I read until my eyes hurt.

I ordered a bottle that night from a company called Auniva. They made a standardized extract. The bottle had 30 servings. It came from a US facility. They had a 90 day money back guarantee, which I noticed but didn't think much about at the time.

It came in 4 days.

I started taking 2 capsules with my coffee on a Wednesday morning. I marked the day on my kitchen calendar with a small star drawn in pencil.

Here is what I am going to tell you about the next 7 weeks. And I want you to understand that I am telling you what happened to my body, in my house, in my life. I am not telling you what will happen to yours. Every body is different. But I am telling you the truth about mine.

The first 2 weeks I didn't feel anything I could put my finger on. I kept taking the capsules every morning. I drank more water than I had been. I went for a 20 minute walk every day in the cul de sac because the forum lady in Asheville said movement helped support the same systems.

Week 3 I noticed I was sleeping different. Deeper, I think. I'd wake up at 6:20 instead of at 4:45 staring at the ceiling.

Week 4 I picked up the maple syrup jar from the farmer's market and opened it without thinking about it. I didn't realize what I'd done until 10 minutes later. I was making pancakes for Dale. I'd poured the syrup. I'd capped the jar. I'd put it back in the cabinet. I stood there holding a spatula looking at the cabinet and I started laughing.

Dale said "what?"

I said "nothing."

Week 5 I sat down at the piano.

I want to tell you what I played but I don't actually remember. It wasn't a song. It was just my hands on the keys, the way they used to be. Both hands. Right hand carrying the melody, left hand finding the chord shapes underneath. The G sharp my pinky used to flinch away from sat right under my finger the way it used to sit there in 1979 when I was learning Pachelbel for my high school graduation.

I cried at the piano for about 20 minutes.

Banjo came in from the kitchen and put his head on my foot.

Week 6 Maddie was over on a Saturday and we were in the kitchen and she was telling me a long, complicated story about a girl in her class who had brought a rock to show and tell and the rock had broken into pieces in the show and tell box. While she was talking I braided her hair.

I hadn't braided her hair in over a year.

She didn't notice. She was busy with her story. She finished her story and turned around and saw her braid in the mirror by the back door and she said "you did one," and I said "I did," and she went back to telling me about the rock.

Week 7 I went back to Dr. Sheppard for a different reason. Annual blood draw, routine, nothing dramatic.

She had me make a fist again. She had me grip her fingers. She watched me do it.

She said "huh."

I said "what?"

She said "your grip is a lot better than last time. What did you change?"

I said "I started a supplement."

She said "which one?"

I said "Indian gooseberry extract. A company called Auniva."

She wrote it down on the back of her chart.

I'm not telling you Dr. Sheppard is going to recommend this to her other patients. I don't know what she does with the notes she writes on charts. I'm telling you she wrote it down.

That was 8 months ago.

I've been on Auniva's Amla every morning since. 2 capsules with my coffee. I keep the bottle on the counter next to the toaster.

I told Dale about the bathroom 5 months in. I waited until I knew the story had a different ending than the one I was scared of. We were sitting on the back porch in the dark and the crickets were going and I just told him. The button on the blouse. The steering wheel. The half bath. Maddie and the silver key with the blue dot.

He was quiet for a long time.

Then he reached over and took my hand the way he used to when we were 24 and just married and we'd sit on the back porch of our first apartment off Brainerd Road and he'd hold my hand because he thought it was the prettiest thing he'd ever seen.

He said "your hand feels different."

I said "I know."

I am not 32 again. I'm not pretending to be. I'm 57 and my knees still talk to me on the steep part of my driveway and I'm not going to climb the dogwood with Maddie even though she asks me to every time.

But I can hold a marinara jar.

I can braid a 6 year old's hair on the first try.

I can play Pachelbel.

I can open my own bathroom door.

If you're reading this and you've been quietly hiding what's happening to your hands, or your knees, or your shoulder when you reach for the coffee filters on the top shelf, if you have a shelf in your pantry that looks like a CVS aisle and a doctor who keeps telling you it's just your age, I'm not telling you what to do.

I'm telling you what I did.

Auniva's Amla is a standardized extract of Indian gooseberry. 2 capsules a day. 30 servings per bottle. Made in the US. Their guarantee is 90 days. Which means you take it for 3 months, and if your body doesn't respond, you mail it back and they refund you. No phone calls. No conversations. No making your case to a customer service person who can't help you.

3 months is a longer trial than most of the bottles in my CVS pantry ever gave me.

P.S. The pearl button on the navy blouse, the small one at the top of the collar that I gave up on in 2023, I buttoned it last week without thinking about it. I was getting ready for church and I stood in front of the mirror and my fingers did what they used to do. I almost called Dale into the room to show him. Then I didn't. Some things are just for you.

P.P.S. If your husband has been quietly opening jars for you for the last few years without saying anything, he knows. He's not pretending. He's just being kind. The kind of man who's been married to you long enough to know when not to ask. That's love too. But you don't have to make him keep doing it. You can let your hands do their own work again.

P.P.P.S. Auniva's Amla has a 90 day money back guarantee. 3 full months. If your hands don't change, if your knees don't loosen, if you don't notice something giving way in the corners of your day that used to be hard, you send it back. The bottles on my CVS pantry shelf didn't come with that. The CBD cream didn't. The magnetic bracelet didn't. Think about who's confident enough in their product to stand behind it for 90 days and who's just collecting your $34.99 hoping you forget to cancel.

P.P.P.P.S. Maddie came over yesterday. She's 7 now. She brought a coloring book with a kitten on the cover and we sat at the kitchen table and colored together for almost an hour. She picked the green crayon for the kitten's grass and the orange for the kitten and she handed me the purple one for the sky because she said "GiGi, you do the sky, you do skies the best." I held that purple crayon in my hand like it was nothing. Like it had always been nothing. The way it should be.

Don't wait for a 6 year old to slide a key under a door.

body.text: {{product.brand}}

Every week I'm off the wall, I can feel my fingers getting weaker.

Grip strengtheners just give you something to squeeze. Hangboards just give you something to hang off. Neither one feels anything like climbing — and honestly, both are boring.

What I actually missed was having a route to solve.

The Boulder Block is a mini climbing wall made from the same holds you're pulling on at the gym, so your fingers work in all the same positions. The graded cards give you real problems to send: lose your grip, shift your fingers, rethink the sequence, go again.

That's what builds contact strength. And it's hard — I've handed it to climbers at the gym who wouldn't give it back until they'd solved the card.

Stronger fingers are just the side effect. What I'm really holding onto is the version of me the wall made.

Over 10,000 climbers have one now, which is exactly why there are so many cheap knockoffs. Get the original — 60-day guarantee.

💪 If your grip gets stronger, your gripper should get harder too.

Adjust the resistance, set the grip to fit your hand, and let the built-in counter track every rep.

🎛️ Adjustable resistance
✋ Adjustable grip width
🔢 Built-in rep counter
🔋 No batteries or app needed
🎒 Compact for home, gym or office

Start easy. Turn it up as you progress.

Squeeze. Count. Get stronger.

My daughter's been climbing for 3 years, and I have never once got her Christmas present right.

Chalk bag — she already had two. Grip strengthener — "too boring," apparently.

So last November, when I kept seeing the Boulder Block, I thought: finally. Put it in my cart. And then left it there, because that's what I do.

By the time I went back, it was sold out. Wasn't going to land before Christmas.

So I panicked and bought a cheap copy on Amazon for about half the price, wrapped it, and stuck a note on it: "Not your actual gift, just a placeholder." Which, looking back, is such a ridiculous thing to do.

The real one turned up 2 days before Christmas. So now there were two under the tree.

You don't have to look hard to tell them apart. The real one is solid wood — you can feel the weight. Real climbing holds, same texture as the ones at her gym. The knockoff is hollow, sounds like a toy when you knock it, and your fingers slide straight off. The real one came with a deck of route cards, easy all the way up to expert. The fake came with nothing. It's just a block.

She picked up the real one and didn't look up again all morning. The fake one's been in a drawer for a year.

So if you've got a climber to buy for and you always leave it to the last minute: order early, and get it from the link below so you know it's the real one. 60 days to send it back if it flops.
